VITALIS — Vital Intelligence and Tracking for Health Systems

VITALIS is a multidisciplinary team driven by innovation, scientific curiosity, and the ambition to develop technology-driven solutions to real-world challenges. We aim to combine research, creativity, engineering, and collaborative problem-solving to explore innovative approaches to healthcare and human well-being.

Our team brings together individuals with diverse skills and perspectives, united by a shared interest in space science
summary: ARCHONS is an astronaut health-monitoring concept designed to support crew health and well-being during space missions. It aims to bring important health indicators and monitoring information into one organized interface, helping users understand health conditions, observe trends, and identify information that may require attention. The project focuses on making health data easier to interpret through a clear dashboard, accessible visualizations, and an intuitive user experience. By combining technology, thoughtful interface design, and health-focused monitoring, ARCHONS explores how digital tools can contribute to safer and more informed human space exploration.
details: Project VITALIS – Vital Intelligence and Tracking for Health Systems What does it do or how does it work? VITALIS is a proposed astronaut health-monitoring platform designed to support long-duration space missions. It brings 3D human anatomy visualization and multiple physiological monitoring modules into one unified interface. It covers cardiovascular, respiratory, neurological, musculoskeletal and other health-related parameters. The platform is designed to receive data from wearable sensors, medical devices and cabin monitoring systems through future hardware and backend integrations. It also distinguishes between live, simulated, sample and unavailable data to maintain transparency. What benefits does it have? VITALIS provides a centralized view of astronaut health information, making it easier to understand physiological changes and monitor different body systems. Its interactive 3D anatomy engine helps users explore individual anatomical structures and connect health information with the human body. Its modular design supports future sensor integration, research analysis and data export. It can also help researchers study long-term physiological changes associated with spaceflight. What is the intended impact of the project? Our goal is to contribute to safer and more informed long-duration human spaceflight. VITALIS aims to provide a foundation for understanding astronaut health trends, supporting research and improving access to organized physiological information. In the future, it could be expanded with validated sensors, backend services and analytical models to support astronaut health research during deep-space missions. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use? The frontend prototype uses React 19, TypeScript, Three.js and WebGL. We use the BodyParts3D 4.0 anatomical reference dataset to provide detailed 3D human anatomy visualization. The proposed hardware architecture includes ESP32 microcontrollers, wearable sensors and BLE, Serial or WebSocket communication interfaces. These are planned integration capabilities rather than a fully deployed physical monitoring system. How is your project creative? The creative aspect of VITALIS is its combination of interactive 3D human anatomy, physiological monitoring and mission-related information in one platform. Instead of presenting health parameters as disconnected numbers, it aims to connect them with anatomical structures and relevant body systems. Its 14 operational modules, interactive anatomy explorer and transparent data-provenance system make the interface extensible and research-oriented. What factors did your team consider? Our team considered the physiological challenges of microgravity, radiation exposure, isolation, mission duration and limited medical resources. We also considered sensor accuracy, signal quality, hardware limitations, data security, privacy, system reliability and future scalability. An important design principle was to clearly distinguish simulated or sample data from actual physical sensor readings. We also recognized that clinical validation, hardware integration and mission-environment testing are necessary before real-world medical use. Current development status: VITALIS is a substantial frontend research prototype. Physical sensor integration, production backend services and clinical validation remain future development goals.
